newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: UNHCR says Bangladesh agrees to abide by rules.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR says Bangladesh agrees to abide by rules.

text.p: The U.N. relief agency UNHCR said on Sunday it had won a commitment from Bangladesh to halt the forcible repatriation of Burmese Moslem refugees.

"The government (of Bangladesh) told us there will be no more forcible repatriation," Canh Nguyen-Tang, UNHCR coordinator for the Bangladesh/Burma repatriation, told reporters after meeting officials in Dhaka.
Bangladesh and the U.N. agency have been at loggerheads over the repatriation of the "Rohingya" refugees.

The repatriations resumed on July 20 after Burmese authorities cleared 7,000 of some 21,000 Rohingya refugees, the remnants of 250,000 who entered Bangladesh in 1992 to escape alleged military persecution in their home province of Arakan in west Burma.
The government postponed the repatriation later that day after sending back nearly 400 people, following clashes between militant refugees and police and a strong protest by the UNHCR to Bangladesh.
Nearly 20 refugees and policemen were injured in the clashes. Police later arrested some 20 militants.
The militants handed a list of conditions for their return to Bangladeshi officials on Saturday.

They said they would only go back if Rangoon issued them with formal nationality documents, restored democracy, handed power to National League for Democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi, and guaranteed human rights.
Bangladesh's Acting Foreign Secretary Aminul Islam earlier told Reuters the government was trying to return the 7,000 refugees by August 15, the deadline set by the Burmese authorities.

The fate of the other 14,000 refugees was uncertain as Burmese authorities had said they could not "trace the identity of 9,000 and that the rest 5,000 have been identified as having genuine causes to be refugees," Nguyen-Tang said without elaborating.
Earlier, the UNHCR had proposed that the 21,000 Rohingyas be allowed to stay in Bangladesh, but Dhaka turned this suggestion down.
UNHCR officials said the resumption of repatriations depended on the restoration of normality in the refugee camps.
"Refugees immediately needed to be assured that there will be no more (use of) force in repatriation. This will help defuse the tension," said Van To Nguyen, a local UNHCR representative.
Thousands of Burmese refugees in Bangladesh are on the verge of starvation because their leaders have forced them to reject government-provided rations, officials said on Sunday.
The militants have even told mothers to keep their children away from camp feeding centres, one relief official told Reuters.
